9:34.devotion: The man born blind had received a miracle, yet the religious leaders refused to celebrate. Instead of rejoicing, they insulted him and expelled him from the synagogue. Sometimes standing with the truth of what God has done costs us standing in our community.
9:34.reflection: Have you ever faced rejection for simply believing or testifying to what God has done in your life?
9:34.action: If you have been shunned or dismissed for your faith, write down one truth about God you will hold onto today instead of hiding.
9:34.prayer: Lord, rejection hurts, even when it comes from religious people. Help me remember that Your approval matters more than anyone's acceptance. Give me courage to stand by the truth of what You have done for me. Amen.

9:35.devotion: Cast out by the religious leaders, the healed man was not left alone. Jesus heard what happened and went looking for him. This verse shows a Savior who seeks out those whom others have pushed away and invites them deeper into faith.
9:35.reflection: When you feel abandoned or excluded, do you trust that Jesus comes looking for you?
9:35.action: Reach out today to someone who may feel excluded from a group or community, and let them know they are not forgotten.
9:35.prayer: Jesus, thank You that when others walk away, You come to find me. Teach me to believe in You more deeply, even in seasons when people let me down. Make me alert to those who need Your seeking love. Amen.

9:36.devotion: Asked whether he believes in the Son of God, the man responds with honest, humble questioning: who is He, that I may believe? Faith often begins with sincere questions. He wanted to know whom to trust, and he asked the One standing before him.
9:36.reflection: What honest questions about Jesus are you carrying, and are you willing to bring them to Him directly?
9:36.action: Write down one sincere question you have about faith, and bring it to God in prayer before you end the day.
9:36.prayer: Lord Jesus, You welcome my questions and do not turn away from my honesty. Give me the humility to ask what I do not know, and the openness to believe when You reveal Yourself. Draw me closer to You today. Amen.

9:37.devotion: Jesus answers the man's question directly: the One he has been speaking with is the Son of God. The man who once was blind now sees, physically and spiritually, and recognizes Jesus face to face. Revelation comes when we meet Jesus personally.
9:37.reflection: Do you recognize that Jesus is not distant, but present and speaking into your life right now?
9:37.action: Set aside ten quiet minutes today to acknowledge Jesus' presence, thanking Him for one specific way He has opened your eyes.
9:37.prayer: Jesus, You are nearer than I often realize. Thank You for opening my eyes, little by little, to who You are. Help me recognize Your presence in ordinary moments today and respond with trust and worship. Amen.

9:38.devotion: The man born blind had just heard Jesus identify Himself as the Son of God. In response, he declared his faith openly and worshiped Jesus. His simple trust stands in contrast to the religious leaders who refused belief despite the evidence before them.
9:38.reflection: When did I last respond to Jesus with the wholehearted worship this man showed?
9:38.action: Today, set aside five quiet minutes to tell Jesus directly that you believe in Him and to worship Him in prayer.
9:38.prayer: Lord Jesus, I believe in You. Open my eyes to see You more clearly, and receive my worship today. Keep my heart simple and trusting, like this man who found You and worshiped. Amen.

9:39.devotion: Jesus explains the effect of His coming: a judgment takes place as people respond to Him. Those who admit their spiritual blindness receive sight, while those who confidently claim they see, yet reject Him, remain in darkness. Humility is the doorway to understanding.
9:39.reflection: Am I willing to admit where I am spiritually blind so Jesus can give me sight?
9:39.action: Identify one area where you have assumed you already know best, and honestly ask God to open your eyes there today.
9:39.prayer: Father, I come to You admitting I do not see everything clearly. Where pride has made me blind, give me humility. Shine Your light into my understanding through Jesus, who came to open blind eyes. Amen.

9:40.devotion: Some Pharisees overheard Jesus' words and took offense, asking whether He considered them blind too. Their question reveals defensiveness rather than honest seeking. They felt secure in their religious standing and were unwilling to consider their need for the light Jesus offered.
9:40.reflection: Do I respond to conviction with honest questions, or with defensiveness that protects my pride?
9:40.action: When someone offers correction today, resist defending yourself immediately; instead listen fully and thank them before considering it.
9:40.prayer: Lord, protect me from a defensive heart that cannot receive Your truth. When Your word challenges me, help me ask honest questions rather than guarded ones. Teach me to welcome Your correction with a soft spirit. Amen.

9:41.devotion: Jesus tells the Pharisees that claiming to see while rejecting Him leaves their sin remaining. If they genuinely did not know, they would not be guilty in the same way; but their refusal to acknowledge their need, while asserting their own insight, kept them in guilt.
9:41.reflection: Where might I be claiming spiritual confidence that keeps me from acknowledging my real need for Jesus?
9:41.action: Write down one way you have relied on your own religious certainty, and confess it honestly to God in prayer today.
9:41.prayer: Father, keep me from the blindness of self-assurance. I do not want to claim I see while remaining in darkness. Expose my pride, forgive my sin, and lead me into honest, humble reliance on Jesus. Amen.

10:1.devotion: Jesus opens a teaching about shepherds and sheepfolds, contrasting two ways of approaching the sheep. One who enters by the door is legitimate; one who climbs over the wall has no rightful claim and intends harm. Jesus is drawing a clear line between trustworthy leadership and exploitative, self-serving pretenders who endanger God's people.
10:1.reflection: Whose voice am I letting shape my life, and how can I tell whether it deserves my trust?
10:1.action: Consider one voice shaping your decisions this week. Test it against Scripture and honest counsel before following it further.
10:1.prayer: Lord Jesus, protect me from voices that would use me rather than serve me. Give me discernment to recognize what is true and safe, and keep my heart near You, the rightful Shepherd of my soul. Amen.

10:2.devotion: Here Jesus identifies the legitimate shepherd by the way he comes—through the door. This pictures rightful, accountable access to the flock. In contrast to those who seize influence secretly or deceitfully, the true shepherd comes openly and has genuine standing with the sheep and with the doorkeeper.
10:2.reflection: Do I trust that Jesus has rightful, complete authority over my life rather than treating Him as one influence among many?
10:2.action: Name one area of your life you have kept apart from Jesus' leadership, and invite His guidance into it today.
10:2.prayer: Good Shepherd, You come to me openly and with all authority, yet You lead with care. Help me welcome Your rightful place in every part of my life, holding nothing back from Your gentle rule. Amen.

10:3.devotion: This verse shows the shepherd's intimate knowledge of his sheep. The doorkeeper opens to him, the sheep recognize his voice, and he calls each one by name before leading them out. It is a picture of personal, individual care—not a nameless crowd, but a flock known one by one and guided purposefully.
10:3.reflection: How does it change me today to believe that Jesus knows my name and calls me personally, not as a stranger in a crowd?
10:3.action: Spend five quiet minutes today listening in prayer, imagining yourself called by name and simply being present with the Lord.
10:3.prayer: Lord, You call me by name, and You know me completely. Quiet my heart so I can hear Your voice above the noise of my day, and give me courage to follow where You lead. Amen.

10:4.devotion: The shepherd goes ahead of his sheep rather than merely driving them from behind. He leads by example and presence, walking the path first. The sheep follow because they have learned to recognize his voice through relationship. Familiarity with the shepherd, built over time, becomes the basis of confident, willing following.
10:4.reflection: Am I learning Jesus' voice deeply enough that following Him feels natural rather than forced?
10:4.action: Read a Gospel passage today slowly, noticing how Jesus speaks and acts, to become more familiar with His voice.
10:4.prayer: Jesus, You walk ahead of me and never ask me to go anywhere You have not gone first. Deepen my familiarity with Your voice so that following You becomes my joy. Amen.

10:5.devotion: Sheep will not follow a stranger because they do not know that voice. Jesus teaches that recognizing Him well equips us to recognize what is not of Him. Discernment grows not from studying every danger but from deep acquaintance with the true Shepherd, whose genuine voice His sheep learn to trust and follow.
10:5.reflection: What voices am I allowing to compete with Jesus' voice for my attention and trust?
10:5.action: Identify one input—a feed, show, or conversation—that consistently pulls you from Christ, and reduce or silence it today.
10:5.prayer: Good Shepherd, train my ears to know You so well that strange voices lose their pull on me. Guard my heart from deception and keep me close enough to You to flee from what is false. Amen.

10:6.devotion: John honestly notes that Jesus' listeners did not understand the illustration. Even those standing closest to Jesus sometimes missed His meaning. This reminds us that spiritual understanding is not automatic; it often requires further teaching, patience, and openness. Jesus does not abandon them in their confusion but continues explaining, as the next verses show.
10:6.reflection: When I do not understand what God is saying, do I bring my confusion honestly to Him or give up?
10:6.action: Write down one teaching of Jesus you find puzzling, and ask Him sincerely to help you understand it as you study.
10:6.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You for patiently teaching even when we do not understand at first. Give me humility to admit my confusion and persistence to keep listening until Your meaning becomes clear. Amen.

10:7.devotion: When the listeners miss the point, Jesus restates it plainly: He Himself is the door of the sheep. The image shifts from shepherd to door, meaning Jesus is the rightful entry point into safety, provision, and life with God. Access to the Father's care comes through Him personally, not through any alternate route.
10:7.reflection: Am I trying to reach God, peace, or belonging through some way other than Jesus?
10:7.action: Bring one striving effort to earn God's acceptance to Jesus in prayer today, and rest in Him as your access to the Father.
10:7.prayer: Jesus, You are the door—the way I come to the Father. Forgive me for the side routes I sometimes chase, and draw me back to enter through You alone, trusting Your welcome. Amen.

10:8.devotion: Jesus contrasts Himself with all who came before as false claimants—those who exploited God's people with self-serving agendas rather than pointing to God faithfully. The sheep, God's true people, did not ultimately follow such deceivers. God preserved a people who recognized and awaited the genuine Shepherd when He appeared.
10:8.reflection: How can I stay rooted in Christ so that grand-sounding but false teachings do not lead me astray?
10:8.action: Compare one teaching you have heard recently with Scripture today, letting the Bible—not popularity—decide whether it is trustworthy.
10:8.prayer: Father, thank You for preserving Your people and sending Your Son, the true Shepherd. Keep me anchored in Your Word so that impressive but empty voices cannot steal my trust or lead my heart away from Christ. Amen.

10:9.devotion: In this passage, Jesus pictures Himself as the door of the sheepfold. In ancient shepherding, the sheep entered through one access point to find safety and provision. Jesus declares that He Himself is that entry: salvation comes through Him alone, and those who come through Him find both security inside and freedom to go in and out, nourished like sheep finding pasture.
10:9.reflection: Am I looking to Jesus as my only way into a safe and flourishing life with God?
10:9.action: Today, bring one worry to Jesus in prayer before trying to solve it on your own strength.
10:9.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You for being the door. Help me stop trying to force my own way into peace and safety. I enter through You today. Lead me to green pastures, and guard my going out and my coming in. Amen.

10:10.devotion: Jesus draws a sharp contrast between two voices competing for our trust. The thief's agenda is taking: he steals, kills, and destroys. Jesus' agenda is giving: He came to offer life, and not bare existence but life in overflowing fullness. Knowing who stands behind each voice helps us choose whom to follow.
10:10.reflection: Which voice has been shaping your daily choices lately—the one that takes, or the One who gives?
10:10.action: Identify one habit or thought pattern that is draining your joy, and intentionally replace that time today with something that nourishes your faith.
10:10.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You for coming to give abundant life. Guard me from the thief's lies, and help me trust Your voice today, walking in the fullness You freely offer. Amen.

10:11.devotion: Jesus continues His shepherd imagery, contrasting Himself with those who serve only for pay. A good shepherd, He says, gives His life for the sheep. This is a striking claim: Jesus is not merely a guide or teacher but a Savior whose care for His people goes all the way to sacrifice. His death on the cross was the ultimate expression of a shepherd's love.
10:11.reflection: Do I trust that Jesus' care for me is so deep He was willing to die for me?
10:11.action: Write down one way you can sacrificially care for someone today, then follow through on it.
10:11.prayer: Good Shepherd, You gave Your life for me when I could not save myself. Teach me to receive that love without earning it, and to love others with even a small measure of the same self-giving heart. Amen.

10:12.devotion: Jesus warns about hirelings—workers with no real ownership or love for the sheep. When danger comes, like a wolf attacking, the hireling flees and the flock is scattered. Jesus is describing unfaithful leaders who abandon people in crisis. The picture helps us see the difference between self-serving leadership and the shepherd who stays when it costs him something.
10:12.reflection: Whose voice am I following—someone who runs when things get hard, or the Shepherd who stays?
10:12.action: Encourage someone today whose trusted leader or friend has let them down, reminding them Jesus never abandons His own.
10:12.prayer: Father, thank You for a Shepherd who does not flee when trouble comes. Guard me from voices that vanish in hard times, and help me be a steady, faithful presence for the people You have placed in my life. Amen.

10:13.devotion: This verse explains the hireling's motive: he runs because he is a hireling and does not care about the sheep. His heart was never in the work. Jesus uses this contrast to reveal His own heart—His commitment flows from genuine love, not obligation or wages. It invites us to examine what motivates our own service to others.
10:13.reflection: When I serve others, is it from genuine care or merely from duty, convenience, or reward?
10:13.action: Do one act of kindness today with no acknowledgment, credit, or repayment expected at all.
10:13.prayer: Lord, forgive me for the times my care for others has been shallow or self-serving. Shape my heart until I love people the way You love them—patiently, sincerely, and without keeping score. Make my care real. Amen.

10:14.devotion: Jesus repeats that He is the good shepherd, and adds a beautiful truth: He knows His sheep, and His sheep know Him. This is not distant awareness but intimate, personal knowledge, like a shepherd naming each animal in his flock. Being known by Jesus means we are never anonymous to God, and knowing Him means our lives are shaped by His voice.
10:14.reflection: Do I live each day aware that the Good Shepherd knows me personally and completely?
10:14.action: Spend ten quiet minutes today simply listening in prayer, asking Jesus to make His voice familiar to you.
10:14.prayer: Good Shepherd, You know me—my name, my fears, my hopes—and still You call me Yours. Help me grow to know You just as personally. Tune my ears to Your voice above every other sound in my life. Amen.

10:15.devotion: Here Jesus compares His relationship with His sheep to His relationship with the Father: just as the Father knows Him, He knows the Father, and He lays down His life for the sheep. His sacrificial love flows from the deepest relationship that exists—the mutual knowledge of Father and Son. Our shepherd's care is rooted in the very heart of God.
10:15.reflection: How does it change me to know Jesus' love for me flows from His own communion with the Father?
10:15.action: Thank God in writing today for three specific ways His care has been personal in your life this year.
10:15.prayer: Father, thank You that Your love for me is not distant or generic, but rooted in Your own knowing of Your Son. Draw me into that fellowship. Let me rest in a care that flows from Your very heart. Amen.

10:16.devotion: Jesus speaks of other sheep not of this fold—gentiles and outsiders beyond Israel—whom He must also bring. They will hear His voice, and there will be one flock with one shepherd. This verse anticipates the gospel going to all nations and the Church made of every background, united not by culture or race but by belonging to Christ.
10:16.reflection: Do I welcome as family in Christ people whose background, culture, or story is different from mine?
10:16.action: Reach out today to a fellow believer whose background differs from yours—share a meal, a call, or an encouraging word.
10:16.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You that Your fold is wider than my comfort zone. You died to gather one flock from every nation and kind of person. Give me Your heart for those I would not naturally call my own. Amen.

10:17.devotion: Jesus says the Father loves Him because He lays down His life in order to take it up again. His sacrifice is not defeat but willing obedience that leads to resurrection. The cross and the empty tomb belong together: the Father delights in the Son's self-giving love, and that love is vindicated in Jesus rising again with life to give His sheep.
10:17.reflection: Do I see Jesus' sacrifice as willing love leading to resurrection, not merely as a tragic loss?
10:17.action: Share with one person today how Jesus' willing sacrifice and resurrection gives you hope in a current struggle.
10:17.prayer: Father, thank You for loving Your Son's obedience, and for raising Him to life again. Because Jesus laid down His life and took it up, I have a living hope. Help me live today in the light of that resurrection. Amen.

10:18.devotion: In the Good Shepherd discourse, Jesus declares that His life is not seized from Him but freely given. He willingly lays down His life for the sheep and has authority to take it up again, according to the Father's command. His sacrifice is deliberate, loving, and victorious.
10:18.reflection: Do I trust that Christ's sacrifice was a free gift of love given for me?
10:18.action: Take a few minutes today to thank God in writing for three specific ways Christ's willing sacrifice has shaped your life.
10:18.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You for laying down Your life willingly for me. Help me live today in gratitude for such deliberate, self-giving love, and to trust the Father's good plan shown in Your death and resurrection. Amen.

10:19.devotion: Jesus' bold claims about His voluntary death and authority caused a stir. His words divided His listeners: some were drawn to believe, others hardened in opposition. Wherever the truth of who Jesus is goes, it demands a response and stirs hearts either toward faith or away from it.
10:19.reflection: When I hear Jesus' claims, do I respond with openness of heart or with resistance?
10:19.action: Notice today where Jesus' words challenge you, and instead of brushing them aside, sit honestly with one area He may be calling you to change.
10:19.prayer: Father, Your Son's words still divide hearts. Soften mine. Where I resist Your truth, give me humility to listen and courage to believe. Draw me closer to Jesus rather than pushing Him away. Amen.

10:20.devotion: Many listeners dismissed Jesus outright, accusing Him of having a demon and being out of His mind, and urged others to stop listening. It is a sobering picture of how strong prejudice can close eyes to the very evidence of God standing before them.
10:20.reflection: Have I ever dismissed someone, or even Jesus Himself, because of assumptions rather than honest listening?
10:20.action: Choose one person you have unfairly dismissed and give them a genuine, respectful hearing today, listening before judging.
10:20.prayer: Lord, guard me from the pride that dismisses truth before hearing it. Give me a listening heart toward You and toward the people around me, so that prejudice never blinds me to what You are saying. Amen.

10:21.devotion: Not everyone rejected Jesus. Some listeners reasoned carefully: His words did not sound like a madman's, and a demon could not open the eyes of the blind. They weighed His words and His works together and began to sense the truth. Faith often begins with honest consideration of the evidence.
10:21.reflection: Am I paying attention to what Jesus' words and works reveal about Him, or merely following the crowd?
10:21.action: Read one Gospel account of Jesus' words and works this evening and simply note what it shows you about who He is.
10:21.prayer: Father, thank You that Your Son's words and works give reason to believe. Give me clear eyes and an honest heart to weigh who Jesus truly is, and lead me to deeper, steadier faith in Him. Amen.

10:22.devotion: The scene shifts to the Feast of Dedication in winter, a festival remembering the purification of the temple. Into that atmosphere of remembered deliverance, Jesus walks again in Jerusalem's temple. The setting quietly underscores the tension building around Him as opposition gathers in the very place devoted to God.
10:22.reflection: How does remembering God's past faithfulness shape the way I respond to Him in my present circumstances?
10:22.action: Recall one specific way God has carried you through a hard season and share that memory with someone today as encouragement.
10:22.prayer: Faithful God, You have delivered Your people before, and You are with us still. As I remember Your past faithfulness, strengthen me to meet present seasons with trust in You. Keep my heart devoted to You. Amen.

10:23.devotion: Jesus walked openly in the temple, in Solomon's porch, a public colonnade where people gathered. He did not hide. Though His life was increasingly in danger, He continued teaching and present among the people, steady and unafraid in His Father's house.
10:23.reflection: Where in my life am I tempted to hide my faith in Jesus rather than live it openly and graciously?
10:23.action: Find one natural, gracious way today to let someone see your faith, such as a kind word, an offered prayer, or an honest mention of what God means to you.
10:23.prayer: Lord Jesus, You walked openly and did not hide Yourself. Give me the same quiet courage to live my faith genuinely among others, not for show, but as a faithful witness to Your love. Amen.

10:24.devotion: Surrounded at the temple, the crowd pressed Jesus to state plainly whether He was the Christ. They wanted a declaration on their terms, yet Jesus knew their hearts were not truly seeking. He had told them, and His works already testified. The obstacle was not unclear words, but unbelieving hearts.
10:24.reflection: Is there something God has already made clear to me that I keep asking about because I do not want to obey it?
10:24.action: Identify one thing you already know God wants you to do, and take its first concrete step today instead of waiting for more clarity.
10:24.prayer: Father, forgive me for asking for more light when I have not walked in the light You have given. Give me a believing heart that responds to Your Son's testimony and obeys what You have already shown me. Amen.

10:25.devotion: Jesus answered that He had already told them who He was, and that the works He did in His Father's name bore witness to Him. His miracles, His compassion, His obedience, all pointed to His identity. Unbelief, Jesus shows, is often not a lack of evidence but a refusal to receive it.
10:25.reflection: What has God already placed in my life that testifies to Him, and am I willing to believe it?
10:25.action: Write down two or three evidences of God's work in your own life this week, and thank Him for each one specifically.
10:25.prayer: Father, thank You that Your Son's works still bear witness to who He is. Open my eyes to see Your hand around me, and turn my wavering questions into settled, obedient faith in Jesus. Amen.

10:26.devotion: In this passage, Jesus is speaking to religious leaders who have questioned Him at the temple. He explains that their unbelief reveals a deeper reality: they are not part of His flock. Belonging to Jesus is not merely about hearing His words outwardly but about trusting Him as His own sheep do.
10:26.reflection: Do I truly trust Jesus, or do I only listen to His words from a distance?
10:26.action: Spend five quiet minutes today honestly asking God to strengthen your trust in Jesus where doubt lingers.
10:26.prayer: Lord Jesus, I want to be counted among Your sheep. Where my heart wavers, draw me closer in faith. Help me believe not just with my ears but with my whole life. Amen.

10:27.devotion: Jesus describes His sheep with three tender markers: they hear His voice, He knows them, and they follow Him. This is a picture of relationship, not mere religion. The Shepherd and His sheep share mutual knowledge, and following Him is the daily fruit of being known and loved by Him.
10:27.reflection: In what ways am I learning to recognize and follow the voice of Jesus above other voices?
10:27.action: Choose one daily habit today, like reading a Gospel passage, that helps you listen for Jesus's voice.
10:27.prayer: Good Shepherd, thank You that You know me by name. Tune my ears to Your voice amid the noise of life, and give me courage to follow You faithfully today. Amen.

10:28.devotion: Jesus describes Himself as the Shepherd who holds His sheep with a grip no power can break. Eternal life is His gift, not something we earn or maintain by our own strength. Because the keeping depends on Him rather than on us, His followers can rest secure. Our safety lies not in how tightly we cling to Him, but in how firmly He holds us.
10:28.reflection: When doubts about your security in Christ arise, where do you look for assurance?
10:28.action: Write this promise on a card and place it where you will see it, reading it aloud whenever worry about your salvation arises today.
10:28.prayer: Good Shepherd, thank You for the gift of life that lasts forever and for Your strong, unfailing hold on me. When fear whispers that I could slip away, remind me that I am safe in Your hand. Teach me to rest there today. Amen.

10:29.devotion: Jesus grounds the security of His flock in the greatness of the Father. The One who gave the sheep to the Son is greater than every power in heaven or earth. Because they rest in the Father's hand, no one is able to snatch them away, a word of deep comfort to troubled hearts.
10:29.reflection: When I feel vulnerable or afraid, do I remember that I am held by a hand no one can overpower?
10:29.action: Write down one fear today and place it visibly in God's hands in prayer, trusting Him with it.
10:29.prayer: Father, thank You that Your hand holds me fast and is greater than anything that threatens me. When I feel weak, remind me that my security rests in Your strength, not mine. Amen.

10:30.devotion: Jesus declares, "I and My Father are one," claiming unity with the Father in nature and purpose. This statement stands at the heart of John's Gospel, where Jesus reveals His divine identity. It is a solemn, glorious claim that anchors the safety of the flock in the oneness of Father and Son.
10:30.reflection: How does Jesus's unity with the Father shape the way I worship and trust Him?
10:30.action: Today, speak or write a one-sentence declaration of your faith in Jesus as one with the Father.
10:30.prayer: Lord Jesus, I worship You as truly one with the Father. Thank You for revealing God to us so plainly. Deepen my awe and trust in You today, my Savior and my God. Amen.

10:31.devotion: The response to Jesus's claim is immediate hostility: His hearers pick up stones to stone Him. This scene shows how strongly His claim to oneness with God provoked opposition. The narrative reminds us that Jesus's identity was never a mild matter; it demanded a verdict from every listener.
10:31.reflection: How do I respond when Jesus's claims challenge my assumptions or cost me something?
10:31.action: Identify one area where you resist Jesus's lordship today and surrender it to Him in prayer.
10:31.prayer: Lord, keep my heart soft toward You. When Your claims confront me, spare me from hardness or hostility. Give me a spirit that welcomes Your truth, even when it unsettles me. Amen.

10:32.devotion: Jesus calmly asks why they would stone Him after all the good works He has done from the Father. His question exposes the inconsistency of opposing one whose life displayed God's mercy and power. The works He performed were meant to point hearers toward recognizing the Father at work in Him.
10:32.reflection: Do I evaluate Jesus by His words alone, or do I also see the goodness of His works?
10:32.action: Read one Gospel account of Jesus's healing or compassion today and note what it reveals about the Father.
10:32.prayer: Father, open my eyes to see Your goodness in the works of Jesus. Let His compassion and power shape my picture of You, and grow my faith in the One You sent. Amen.

10:33.devotion: His opponents explain themselves plainly: they are not stoning Him for a good work, but for blasphemy, because He, a man, was making Himself God. They understood exactly what Jesus claimed. The passage shows that the early conflict over Jesus centered precisely on His divine identity, not a misunderstanding.
10:33.reflection: Do I take Jesus's claim to deity as seriously as His first hearers did?
10:33.action: Today, thank Jesus in a specific prayer for who He is, not only for what He has done for you.
10:33.prayer: Lord Jesus, You did not merely teach or do good; You claimed to be God. I believe Your claim. Help me live today in light of Your true identity as my Lord. Amen.

10:34.devotion: Jesus answers from the Hebrew Scriptures, citing Psalm 82, where human judges are addressed as "gods" in their role as bearers of God's word. His argument is that if Scripture could speak this way of humans entrusted with divine authority, His own claim, backed by the Father, deserves a fair hearing.
10:34.reflection: Do I let Scripture speak fully before I rush to judge what Jesus says?
10:34.action: Read Psalm 82 today and consider how Jesus used Scripture to invite His hearers to honest examination.
10:34.prayer: Father, thank You that Jesus engaged His critics with Scripture, not anger. Give me a love for Your Word, patience with those who differ, and a heart willing to examine truth honestly. Amen.

10:35.devotion: When accused of blasphemy for calling Himself God's Son, Jesus answered from Scripture, noting that God's word addressed human judges as 'gods' in the Psalms. His argument rests on a settled conviction: Scripture cannot be broken. God's word is trustworthy, enduring, and never fails to accomplish its purpose.
10:35.reflection: Do I treat Scripture as unbreakable truth that shapes how I think and decide?
10:35.action: Choose one Bible passage today and let it guide one actual decision you face, however small.
10:35.prayer: Lord, thank You for a word that cannot be broken. Root my heart in Your Scriptures, teach me to trust them fully, and shape my thoughts and choices by Your unchanging truth. In Jesus' name, Amen.

10:36.devotion: Jesus contrasted His critics' accusation with His Father's commission. The Father had sanctified Him, set Him apart and sent Him into the world. To reject the One God consecrated and sent, while claiming to honor God, was the deeper inconsistency Jesus exposed to His opponents.
10:36.reflection: Am I willing to receive Jesus on the Father's terms rather than my own expectations?
10:36.action: Write a short note of thanks to God for sending Jesus, and share one reason for that gratitude with someone today.
10:36.prayer: Father, You set apart Your Son and sent Him into the world. Thank You for that gift. Keep me from hard-hearted objections, and give me a humble heart that receives Jesus as Your Son. Amen.

10:37.devotion: Jesus invited honest examination rather than blind demand for belief. He said that if He did not do the Father's works, His hearers should not believe Him. Faith in Jesus, He showed, is not irrational; it responds to real evidence of God's presence and power at work.
10:37.reflection: Do I examine Jesus' claims honestly, or dismiss them without considering what He actually did?
10:37.action: Read one Gospel account of Jesus' works today and note what it shows about the Father.
10:37.prayer: Lord Jesus, You welcomed honest questions and pointed to Your works. Give me a sincere heart that examines the evidence fairly, and lead my questioning into genuine, grounded faith in You. Amen.

10:38.devotion: Jesus offered a gracious alternative: even if His hearers struggled to believe His words, they could believe the works He performed. Those works pointed to a profound truth, that the Father is in Him and He in the Father. Evidence was meant to lead to relationship, not mere curiosity.
10:38.reflection: When belief feels hard, am I willing to let what God has done lead me to deeper trust?
10:38.action: Recall one concrete way God has worked in your life, and tell someone about it as evidence of His care.
10:38.prayer: Father, when words alone seem difficult to grasp, help me remember Your works. Use them to draw me into knowing You more deeply, until I rest in the truth that the Father and Son are one. Amen.

10:39.devotion: The opposition escalated: Jesus' opponents again tried to seize Him, yet He escaped from their hands. This moment shows both growing hostility toward Him and His sovereign control over His timeline. His hour had not yet come, and no power could take Him before the appointed time.
10:39.reflection: How do I respond when following Jesus meets resistance or hostility?
10:39.action: Identify one situation where you face pressure over your faith, and prayerfully choose a faithful, peaceful response today.
10:39.prayer: Lord Jesus, even hostile hands could not hold You before Your hour came. When I face resistance for following You, steady my heart, guard me from fear, and help me trust Your sovereign timing. Amen.

10:40.devotion: Facing danger, Jesus withdrew across the Jordan to where John first baptized. This was not defeat but deliberate retreat to a fruitful place, a location rich with memory of His forerunner's ministry. Sometimes faithful stewardship of life and mission means stepping back to safer ground for a season.
10:40.reflection: Am I willing to withdraw wisely when needed, without seeing retreat as failure?
10:40.action: Take ten minutes today to step away from pressure, find quiet, and pray about where God wants you serving now.
10:40.prayer: Father, You know when to press forward and when to withdraw. Give me wisdom to recognize both, freedom from false shame in rest, and confidence that Your purposes advance even in quiet seasons. Amen.

10:41.devotion: In that place, many came to Jesus and reflected on John the Baptist. He performed no signs, yet everything he said about Jesus proved true. A faithful witness without spectacular displays still bore lasting fruit, pointing people to Christ through truthful testimony alone.
10:41.reflection: Is my witness marked more by truthful testimony about Jesus than by a desire to impress?
10:41.action: Speak one simple, true sentence about Jesus to someone today, without embellishment or pressure.
10:41.prayer: Lord, thank You for witnesses like John who simply spoke truth about You. Make my testimony honest and plain, and use humble words to draw others to believe in Your Son. Amen.

10:42.devotion: The passage closes with a beautiful outcome: many believed in Him there. Where hostile crowds earlier rejected Jesus, open hearts in a quiet place received Him. Faith often grows in ordinary settings where honest people consider the truth about Christ and respond with trust.
10:42.reflection: Where might God be working quietly around me, inviting people to believe?
10:42.action: Pray by name for one person today who seems far from faith, asking God to open their heart to Jesus.
10:42.prayer: Father, You drew many to believe in quiet places far from contention. Thank You that faith still grows in ordinary moments. Use me to point others to Jesus, and bring many to believe in Him. Amen.

11:1.devotion: This verse opens the well-known account of Lazarus, a man Jesus knew personally. Lazarus lived in Bethany, a small village near Jerusalem, with his sisters Mary and Martha. The story that follows shows Jesus meeting a family in crisis, and it invites us to bring our own emergencies and griefs to Him honestly.
11:1.reflection: When illness or trouble enters my home, do I turn to Jesus first or only as a last resort?
11:1.action: Name one difficult situation in your life today and deliberately bring it to Jesus in specific, spoken prayer.
11:1.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You that You care about the real troubles in my home and family. Teach me to bring every need to You quickly and honestly, trusting You with the people I love. Amen.

11:2.devotion: John reminds readers of Mary's devotion to Jesus, describing her anointing His feet with costly oil and drying them with her hair. Her love for Christ was deep and personal, and her brother's sickness touched someone who knew Jesus intimately. Devotion to Jesus does not shield us from hardship, but it shapes how we face it.
11:2.reflection: Is my love for Jesus expressed in tangible, costly ways, or only in words when life is easy?
11:2.action: Do one concrete act of devotion today, such as extra time in prayer, generous giving, or serving someone quietly in Jesus' name.
11:2.prayer: Father, I want to love Your Son the way Mary did, openly and at real cost. Deepen my devotion so that hardship does not weaken it, and help me serve You with my hands as well as my heart. Amen.

11:3.devotion: The sisters sent word to Jesus with a simple, trusting message: the one He loved was sick. They did not demand a specific response or explain what Jesus should do. Their message shows a humble confidence in His care. We can follow their example, telling Jesus our troubles plainly and leaving the outcome with Him.
11:3.reflection: When I pray about a crisis, am I trusting Jesus with the outcome, or instructing Him on exactly what to do?
11:3.action: Write a one-sentence prayer today that simply states your need to Jesus without adding instructions, then leave it with Him.
11:3.prayer: Lord, I bring You my need just as it is, without demands or instructions. You know my situation and the people I love. I rest my hopes in Your wisdom and Your care. Amen.

11:4.devotion: When Jesus heard His friend was sick, He did not panic or rush away. He reframed the crisis entirely: this illness would not end in final death but would serve God's glory. What looks like tragedy in the moment can become the very stage where God's power and His Son's honor are displayed.
11:4.reflection: Which painful circumstance in your life might God be using to reveal His glory rather than defeat you?
11:4.action: Name one painful situation in your life today and thank God aloud that He can still be glorified through it.
11:4.prayer: Lord Jesus, help me trust You when circumstances frighten me. Take my sickness, sorrow, and fear, and use them for Your glory. Open my eyes to see Your purpose at work even in my hardest days. Amen.

11:5.devotion: Right in the middle of this painful story, John states plainly that Jesus loved Martha, Mary, and Lazarus. This statement anchors the whole chapter: everything that follows unfolds from His love, even when events were confusing and painful to the family. Love and delay will sit side by side in this account, and we are meant to hold both truths together.
11:5.reflection: Can I believe that Jesus loves me even when His response to my prayers is not what I expected?
11:5.action: Memorize this truth today by writing it in your own words and placing it where you will see it during difficult moments.
11:5.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You that Your love for Your friends is stated so plainly. When Your ways confuse me, anchor my heart in that love. Help me trust that You care for me even in the waiting. Amen.

11:6.devotion: Strangely to us, when Jesus heard His friend was sick, He stayed two more days where He was. The text has just told us He loved them, so this delay was not neglect. His timing served a purpose the sisters could not yet see, though the story does not promise every delay will end as this one did.
11:6.reflection: How do I respond when God's timing feels slow and my need feels urgent?
11:6.action: Identify one prayer you have been waiting on, and thank God today for His wisdom even before you see an answer.
11:6.prayer: Father, waiting is hard, especially when someone I love is hurting. Teach me to trust Your timing without demanding quick answers, and to keep praying faithfully while I wait. Sustain me in the delay. Amen.

11:7.devotion: After the delay, Jesus told His disciples they were going back to Judea, toward danger and toward Lazarus. His move was deliberate and purposeful, not hurried by panic or deterred by risk. He moved according to the Father's timing and mission. This verse reminds us that obedience to God sometimes means walking toward hard places, not away from them.
11:7.reflection: Is there a difficult step of obedience I have been avoiding because it feels risky or uncomfortable?
11:7.action: Take one avoided step of obedience today, such as a hard conversation, a confession, or an act of service you have postponed.
11:7.prayer: Lord Jesus, You moved deliberately and without fear. Give me courage to obey You even when the path looks difficult, and to trust Your purposes more than my comfort. Strengthen me for the step You are asking. Amen.

11:8.devotion: The disciples objected, reminding Jesus that people in Judea had recently tried to stone Him. Their concern was understandable; returning genuinely seemed dangerous. Yet their words reveal a mindset focused on threat rather than mission. In facing opposition, we honor God not by seeking danger recklessly, but by not letting fear of it silence obedience.
11:8.reflection: When following Jesus becomes uncomfortable or costly, does fear of opposition outweigh my trust in His leading?
11:8.action: Name one fear that has been holding back your obedience, and share it honestly with a trusted Christian friend or mentor today.
11:8.prayer: Father, I confess that fear of trouble sometimes outweighs my trust in You. Like the disciples, I see danger more clearly than mission. Give me steady courage to follow Christ even when obedience is costly. Amen.

11:9.devotion: Jesus answered the disciples' fear with a picture from daily life: a day has twelve hours, and those who walk in daylight do not stumble because they see. His point, in context, is that He was walking in the light of the Father's will for that day, and that timing was not yet threatened. Walking with God in His appointed time brings clarity, even on a risky road.
11:9.reflection: Am I walking in step with God's will today, or stumbling ahead of Him and behind Him in my own timing?
11:9.action: Before making one decision today, pause and ask God in prayer whether this is His appointed time and way, then act accordingly.
11:9.prayer: Father, You have given me this day to walk with You. Keep me in Your light and Your timing, so I do not stumble ahead in fear or lag behind in doubt. Guide each step today. Amen.

11:10.devotion: Jesus has just declared Himself the light of the world as He prepares to return to Judea despite danger. Walking without light leads to stumbling, He says, because the light is not within the person. As Jesus moves toward the cross, His disciples are invited to follow Him confidently, guided by His presence rather than by fear of the darkness around them.
11:10.reflection: Where am I trying to walk in my own strength instead of following the light of Christ?
11:10.action: Before making today's decisions, pause and ask Jesus to guide each step, especially where the way forward feels uncertain or dark.
11:10.prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the light I need. When the path ahead seems dark and I am tempted to stumble, keep my eyes on You. Lead me today by Your truth, and let me walk confidently in Your presence. Amen.

11:11.devotion: Jesus tells His disciples that Lazarus, their friend, has fallen asleep and that He is going to wake him. In John's Gospel, Jesus speaks this way about death, viewing it from the standpoint of resurrection power. He deliberately delays His journey so that what He will do at the tomb will reveal God's glory and deepen the disciples' faith.
11:11.reflection: Do I believe that Jesus approaches even death itself with the authority to awaken and restore?
11:11.action: Name one situation in your life that feels final or hopeless, and bring it to Jesus in prayer today.
11:11.prayer: Jesus, You called Lazarus Your friend, and You know my name too. Thank You that nothing, not even death, is beyond Your power to awaken. Help me trust You with the situations I have given up on. Amen.

11:12.devotion: The disciples misunderstand Jesus and answer logically: if Lazarus is only sleeping, then rest is exactly what he needs to recover. Their reasonable conclusion misses what Jesus actually means. This small exchange reminds us that even devoted followers of Jesus sometimes hear His words through assumptions rather than receiving the deeper truth He intends to communicate.
11:12.reflection: When I read or hear Jesus' words, do I bring my assumptions, or do I truly listen for what He means?
11:12.action: Choose one Bible passage today and read it slowly twice, asking God to correct any assumptions you bring to it.
11:12.prayer: Father, I confess that I often hear what I expect to hear instead of what You are actually saying. Give me a humble, teachable heart. Open my ears and mind to receive Your truth as it truly is. Amen.

11:13.devotion: John clarifies the scene for readers: Jesus was speaking of Lazarus's death, but the disciples assumed He meant ordinary rest. Their misunderstanding sets up Jesus to speak plainly. Scripture is honest about the disciples' confusion, which encourages us. Following Jesus does not require perfect understanding, but it does invite us to keep listening until He makes things clear.
11:13.reflection: Am I willing to stay close to Jesus and keep asking, even when I do not understand Him at first?
11:13.action: Write down one question about faith you have been avoiding, and bring it honestly to God in prayer today.
11:13.prayer: Lord, thank You that Your disciples did not always understand You, yet You stayed with them and spoke plainly. When I am confused, help me not to walk away but to keep listening until Your truth becomes clear. Amen.

11:14.devotion: Jesus stops speaking figuratively and tells the disciples directly that Lazarus is dead. He does not soften the truth or hide behind vague words. In the face of real loss, Jesus is honest, and His honesty is not cruel but prepares the disciples for what He is about to do. Clear truth becomes the ground on which their faith can grow.
11:14.reflection: Do I let Jesus speak hard truths to me plainly, or do I prefer comfortable illusions?
11:14.action: Speak honestly with God today about one painful reality you have been dressing up in softer words.
11:14.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You that You never deceive me with half-truths. Give me courage to face hard realities honestly, with You beside me. And when the truth is painful, remind me that You are greater than what I fear. Amen.

11:15.devotion: Jesus says He is glad He was not present before Lazarus died, for the disciples' sake, so that they may believe. This is not indifference to grief but a purposeful delay that will set the stage for a greater revelation of His power. Jesus invites His followers to trust that His timing, though mysterious, serves a deeper work than immediate rescue.
11:15.reflection: Can I trust that Jesus' delays in my life might serve a purpose I cannot yet see?
11:15.action: Recall one prayer that seems delayed or unanswered, and commit it afresh to Jesus, asking for faith to trust His timing.
11:15.prayer: Jesus, waiting is hard, and I do not always understand Your timing. Help me believe that You are working even when You seem delayed. Grow my faith in the seasons where I would rather have quick answers. Amen.

11:16.devotion: Thomas, called the Twin, responds to Jesus' decision to return to Judea, where opponents recently threatened to stone Him, with grim loyalty: let us go, that we may die with Him. Though later known for doubting, Thomas here shows devoted courage. His words capture both real love for Jesus and a pessimism that does not yet grasp the resurrection hope Jesus holds.
11:16.reflection: Would I follow Jesus even when following looks costly and the outcome seems hopeless?
11:16.action: Identify one area where following Jesus feels costly to you, and take one small obedient step in that area today.
11:16.prayer: Lord Jesus, give me Thomas's courage to follow You even when the road looks dangerous and the outcome unclear. But give me more than grim loyalty; give me living hope in Your power over every fearful thing. Amen.

11:17.devotion: Jesus arrives in Bethany and finds Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. In Jewish thought of the time, this marked death as thoroughly final, underscoring that no one could claim Lazarus was merely resting. The scene sets the stage: Jesus arrives precisely when human hope has ended, so that what follows can only be attributed to God's power.
11:17.reflection: Where have I concluded it is too late for God to act?
11:17.action: Bring to Jesus one situation you have labeled 'too late,' and pray specifically, asking Him to work in it this week.
11:17.prayer: Father, sometimes hope runs out before Your help arrives. Thank You that Jesus came to the tomb after four days, when everything seemed finished. Teach me that endings I see are not endings to You. Amen.

11:18.devotion: Bethany's closeness to Jerusalem matters here. Jesus is entering the region where His enemies are gathering, near the very city where He will soon face the cross. His journey to this grieving family is not safe or incidental; it is a deliberate act of love that leads Him toward danger and, ultimately, toward His own hour.
11:18.reflection: When has love asked you to move toward someone's pain rather than away from it?
11:18.action: Choose one person whose grief or struggle you have avoided, and take a simple step toward them today: a call, a visit, or a note.
11:18.prayer: Lord Jesus, You did not keep a safe distance from sorrow. Give me courage to draw near to those who hurt, even when it costs me comfort. Make my love as willing as Yours. Amen.

11:19.devotion: In this culture, mourners gathered for days, and many came to comfort Martha and Mary after Lazarus died. Community presence in grief was expected and meaningful. This scene reminds us that sorrow is not meant to be carried alone, and that showing up for the bereaved is a genuine ministry, even before any words of hope are spoken.
11:19.reflection: Whose grief have you hesitated to enter because you did not know what to say?
11:19.action: Reach out to someone who is grieving this week. Offer your presence simply, without trying to fix or explain their loss.
11:19.prayer: Father, thank You for the gift of companions in sorrow. Teach me to comfort others as I would want to be comforted, with patience, presence, and gentle words. Help me show up faithfully. Amen.

11:20.devotion: When word comes that Jesus is near, Martha and Mary respond differently: Martha hurries out to meet Him while Mary stays in the house, seated in her grief. The Gospel quietly honors both responses. Grief moves at different speeds, and Jesus receives each sister where she is, going to Mary just as He came to Martha.
11:20.reflection: In your own sorrow, are you more likely to run toward God with your questions or to sit quietly until He comes to you?
11:20.action: Let your grief or stress meet Jesus honestly today, in whatever posture fits you: speak to Him in prayer, or simply sit quietly with Him for a few minutes.
11:20.prayer: Lord, You meet us in motion and in stillness. Accept me as I am today, whether my faith is bold or my heart can only sit and wait. Come near, as You always do. Amen.

11:21.devotion: Martha's words to Jesus are raw and honest: if You had been here, my brother would not have died. Scripture does not scold her for this. Her complaint is wrapped in trust, because she still comes to Jesus, still calls Him Lord. Honest lament addressed to God is not unbelief; it is faith bringing its deepest ache into His presence.
11:21.reflection: What disappointment with God have you been afraid to say out loud to Him?
11:21.action: Write or speak one honest, unedited prayer to God today, naming your real feelings about a situation that has hurt or confused you.
11:21.prayer: Father, You can handle my honesty. Here is what I have carried quietly: my grief, my questions, my sense of Your absence. Receive it as Martha did her own words, and meet me in the middle of them. Amen.

11:22.devotion: Martha follows her complaint with remarkable faith: even now, she says, she knows God will give Jesus whatever He asks. Even now, with her brother in the tomb, she does not treat the situation as finished. Her words show a faith that holds on past disappointment, trusting Jesus' connection to the Father even when the outcome is not yet visible.
11:22.reflection: Can I say even now in the middle of my hardest circumstance, or does my faith only rise when things improve?
11:22.action: Name one situation you had given up on, and pray over it today with the words even now, asking God to work according to His will.
11:22.prayer: Lord Jesus, even now, in the situation I considered closed, I believe You are able. I do not know what You will do, but I trust You will act rightly. Sustain my hope while I wait. Amen.

11:23.devotion: Jesus tells Martha her brother will rise again. He speaks of a real hope beyond the grave, rooted in God's promise of resurrection. Yet He intends to deepen her understanding: the hope He offers is not an abstract doctrine about a distant future, but a person standing before her, about to demonstrate His power over death itself.
11:23.reflection: Is my hope in resurrection a distant idea, or does it shape how I face loss today?
11:23.action: When you face discouragement today, pause and recall that Christ's promise of resurrection reaches beyond every loss you experience now.
11:23.prayer: Lord, thank You that death is not the end of Your story for those who belong to You. When loss feels final, anchor my heart in Your promise of rising again. Amen.

11:24.devotion: Martha answers with the hope she has learned: she knows her brother will rise in the resurrection at the last day. Her faith is genuine and orthodox, yet Jesus is about to draw her further. He gently moves her from knowing about a future event to trusting Him personally, the one in whom that promised future is grounded.
11:24.reflection: Do I rest in right answers about God, or in God Himself?
11:24.action: Move one belief from your head to your heart today by telling God in prayer that you trust Him personally, not merely the truths you know about Him.
11:24.prayer: Father, I am grateful for everything I have learned of Your truth. Teach me to know You, not just facts about You. Let my faith rest in You, living and near, today and always. Amen.

11:25.devotion: Standing before a grieving sister, Jesus makes one of His great I am declarations: He is the resurrection and the life. The future hope Martha confessed is embodied in Him now. Whoever believes in Him, though they die, shall live. Jesus does not merely promise resurrection; He presents Himself as its very source and guarantee.
11:25.reflection: How would facing my fears of loss change if I truly trusted Jesus as the source of life beyond death?
11:25.action: Memorize this promise of Jesus today, and repeat it to yourself whenever fear of loss or death surfaces in your thoughts.
11:25.prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the resurrection and the life. I believe in You. When death and loss press near, hold me in Your promise that life with You is stronger than the grave. Amen.

11:26.devotion: Speaking with Martha near Bethany after her brother Lazarus has died, Jesus makes a staggering promise: everyone who lives and believes in Him will never truly die. Physical death remains a reality in this world, but for the believer it cannot hold final power. Then He turns the promise into a personal question that still stands before each of us today.
11:26.reflection: Do I believe that Jesus' promise of life reaches even beyond my greatest fears?
11:26.action: Write John 11:25-26's promise in your own words and share it with one person who needs hope today.
11:26.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You that death does not have the last word for those who trust You. Strengthen my faith when grief or fear clouds my vision. Help me answer Your question with an honest, believing yes. Amen.

11:27.devotion: Martha responds to Jesus with one of the clearest confessions in the Gospels. Amid her grief and unanswered questions, she names Him as Lord, as the Christ, and as the Son of God entering the world. Her faith does not depend on having every explanation; it rests on who Jesus is.
11:27.reflection: Can I confess who Jesus is even when my circumstances leave me confused?
11:27.action: Speak aloud a simple confession of faith in Jesus today, naming Him as Lord and Son of God in your own prayer.
11:27.prayer: Jesus, like Martha, I confess You as the Christ, the Son of God. When I cannot understand Your ways, anchor my faith in who You are, not only in what You do. Keep my confession honest and steady. Amen.

11:28.devotion: After her confession, Martha hurries home to tell Mary privately that the Teacher is asking for her. In a time when grieving women were rarely left alone, she quietly makes space for her sister to meet Jesus. Martha's faith quickly becomes an invitation, drawing someone she loves toward the Lord.
11:28.reflection: Who in my grief or struggle needs me to pass along Jesus' invitation?
11:28.action: Contact one grieving or struggling person today with a simple message that Jesus cares and you are praying for them.
11:28.prayer: Lord, thank You for people like Martha who carry Your invitation to others. Make me attentive to friends and family who need to hear that You are calling them. Use my small, quiet words to draw someone closer to You. Amen.

11:29.devotion: When Mary hears that Jesus is asking for her, she rises at once and goes to Him. Her eager response, without hesitation or delay, shows how deeply she trusted the One who called her. In her darkest hour, the sound of the Teacher's voice was reason enough to move.
11:29.reflection: How quickly do I respond when I sense Jesus drawing near to me?
11:29.action: Set aside ten unhurried minutes today to come to Jesus in prayer before attending to anything else on your schedule.
11:29.prayer: Lord Jesus, give me Mary's eagerness. When You call me through Your Word, through prayer, or through circumstances, let me rise quickly and come to You without delay. You are worth my immediate attention. Amen.

11:30.devotion: Jesus remains at the place outside the village where Martha met Him, not yet entering Bethany. This quiet detail reminds us that He often meets people at the edge of their sorrow, on the road, before anything is resolved. He positions Himself where the hurting will pass by on their way to Him.
11:30.reflection: Am I looking for Jesus only in comfortable places, or also on the difficult roads where He waits?
11:30.action: During a walk or commute today, intentionally pray and invite Jesus to meet you in whatever situation feels unresolved.
11:30.prayer: Jesus, thank You that You do not wait for my life to be tidy before meeting me. Meet me on the roads of my unfinished business and unresolved pain, and teach me to recognize Your presence there. Amen.

11:31.devotion: The mourners comforting Mary see her leave quickly and assume she is going to Lazarus's tomb to weep, so they follow her. Their presence shows how thoroughly grief surrounded this family, yet they unknowingly accompany Mary toward a divine encounter. Sometimes sorrow's crowded rooms become the very path to meeting Jesus.
11:31.reflection: When I follow someone in their grief, could God be preparing an encounter I do not yet see?
11:31.action: Accompany or check in on someone walking through sorrow this week, offering your presence without needing to fix anything.
11:31.prayer: Father, thank You for the friends who mourned alongside Mary and Martha. Teach me to be a faithful comforter, present and gentle. Use even ordinary moments of accompanying the grieving to become doorways to Your grace. Amen.

11:32.devotion: Mary reaches Jesus and falls at His feet with the same words her sister spoke earlier: if He had been present, Lazarus would not have died. Her words carry raw honesty and deep faith together. She does not hide her disappointment from Jesus; she brings it directly to Him and worshipfully lays it down.
11:32.reflection: Am I honest with Jesus about my disappointment, or do I hide it behind polite words?
11:32.action: Write a candid prayer today telling Jesus exactly where you feel He seemed absent, then sit quietly with Him afterward.
11:32.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You that I can fall at Your feet with my unfiltered questions and grief. Receive my honest words without my pretending. Meet me in the tension between my disappointment and my trust in You. Amen.

11:33.devotion: Seeing Mary weeping, and the mourners with her, Jesus groans in His spirit and is deeply troubled. He is not a distant observer of human sorrow; He is moved to His depths by it. Before He acts, He feels. The Gospel here reveals a Savior whose compassion engages fully with the pain around Him.
11:33.reflection: Do I trust that Jesus is genuinely moved by my tears, not merely aware of them?
11:33.action: When you encounter someone's pain today, pause and let it touch you before offering advice or moving on with your day.
11:33.prayer: Jesus, thank You that You are not cold or detached from my sorrow. You groaned with the grieving at Bethany, and You draw near to me now. Help me also feel deeply for the hurting people around me. Amen.

11:34.devotion: Standing at the edge of grief, Jesus asks where Lazarus has been laid. He does not rush past the mourners or minimize the loss. Instead, He invites Himself into the very place of sorrow, showing that the Lord is willing to walk with us into our darkest moments.
11:34.reflection: When grief weighs on me, do I trust that Jesus is willing to come close and see it with me?
11:34.action: Reach out today to someone who is grieving, offering your presence rather than answers—perhaps a visit, call, or meal.
11:34.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You that You do not keep me at arm's length in my sorrow. Come into the places where I hurt, and teach me to walk alongside others with Your gentle compassion. Amen.

11:35.devotion: The shortest verse in English Scripture carries profound weight. Jesus, knowing He will raise Lazarus, still weeps at the tomb. His tears show that He genuinely shares the pain of those He loves, and that sorrow and faith in God's power are not contradictions.
11:35.reflection: Do I allow Jesus to meet me not only in my solutions but also in my tears?
11:35.action: Give yourself permission today to feel and express sorrow honestly before God instead of hiding it behind forced cheerfulness.
11:35.prayer: Weeping Savior, thank You for Your tears at the tomb. You understand my grief from the inside. Help me bring my honest sorrow to You, trusting that You never shame me for weeping. Amen.

11:36.devotion: The mourners watching Jesus weep recognize the obvious: He loved Lazarus deeply. Even before any miracle occurs, Jesus's compassion makes His love visible. His tears become a testimony, showing those around Him—and us—that divine love is not distant but tender and real.
11:36.reflection: Would the people around me recognize Christ's love by the way I care for others?
11:36.action: Let someone know plainly today that you love them—speak it or write it in a simple note or message.
11:36.prayer: Father, Your Son's tears showed everyone how much He loved Lazarus. Make my own love that visible and honest. Help me care for people so genuinely that Your kindness is evident through me. Amen.

11:37.devotion: Some in the mourning crowd question why Jesus, famous for healing a blind man, did not prevent Lazarus's death. Their words mix grief with doubt. The passage honestly records such hard questions, reminding us that honest confusion can sit alongside sincere seeking.
11:37.reflection: When God's timing does not match my expectations, do I bring my hard questions to Him honestly?
11:37.action: Write down one honest question or disappointment you have toward God, and share it with Him in prayer today.
11:37.prayer: Lord, You know the questions I carry when Your ways puzzle me. Thank You that You welcome my honesty. Meet me in my confusion and strengthen my trust in Your wisdom and love. Amen.

11:38.devotion: Still groaning deeply within, Jesus approaches the tomb, a cave sealed by a stone. The scene is heavy with finality—death's barrier standing firm. Yet Jesus moves toward it deliberately. He does not avoid the place of death but confronts it directly, preparing to reveal God's power.
11:38.reflection: What sealed stone in my life have I assumed is simply too final for God to address?
11:38.action: Identify one situation you have given up on, and pray over it today, asking God to work even there.
11:38.prayer: Lord Jesus, You walked straight to the tomb, facing death itself without fear. Give me courage to bring even my most hopeless situations to You, believing that no barrier stands beyond Your power. Amen.

11:39.devotion: When Jesus commands that the stone be removed, Martha objects—practically and reasonably, since Lazarus has been dead four days. Her concern is understandable, yet Jesus gently reminds her of what He said: belief opens the way to seeing God's glory. Faith sometimes asks us to act beyond our expectations.
11:39.reflection: Is my practical caution keeping me from obeying what God is asking of me right now?
11:39.action: Take one small step of obedience you have been avoiding, even if it feels awkward or seems pointless.
11:39.prayer: Father, like Martha, I sometimes reason my way out of obedience. Forgive my hesitations. Give me faith to move stones when You ask, trusting that You are working in ways I cannot yet see. Amen.

11:40.devotion: Jesus answers Martha's objection with a gentle reminder of His earlier promise: if she would believe, she would see the glory of God. Faith here is connected to seeing—trust becomes the doorway through which God's power is revealed. The command to remove the stone tests whether she will take Him at His word.
11:40.reflection: What promise of God do I need to remember and act on today, even before I see results?
11:40.action: Recall one Scripture promise that speaks to your current situation, write it out, and pray it back to God today.
11:40.prayer: Lord, help me hold onto Your word even when circumstances argue against it. Strengthen my belief so that I may see Your glory at work, and keep me faithful when obedience requires trust first. Amen.

11:41.devotion: After the stone is removed, Jesus lifts His eyes to heaven and thanks the Father for hearing Him. Before anything happens, He prays with confident gratitude. His prayer models intimacy with the Father and teaches us that thanksgiving belongs in prayer even before we see the answer.
11:41.reflection: Do I thank God for hearing me before I see His answers, or only afterward?
11:41.action: Begin today's prayers with thanksgiving—thank God for three ways He has heard you before making any requests.
11:41.prayer: Father, thank You that You hear me through Your Son. Teach me to pray with Jesus's confidence, beginning with gratitude, trusting that You listen even when the answer has not yet appeared. Amen.

11:42.devotion: Standing at Lazarus's tomb, Jesus prays aloud before raising His friend. He thanks the Father, affirming that God always hears Him, and explains that He prays publicly so the bystanders may believe the Father has sent Him. The prayer is both intimate communion and open testimony, inviting the crowd to witness God's power and trust in Christ.
11:42.reflection: When others hear you pray, do your words point them toward faith in Jesus?
11:42.action: Pray aloud today in a simple, sincere way—a meal, a phone call, or with family—letting your words gently point others to God.
11:42.prayer: Father, thank You that You always hear me through Your Son. Make my prayers honest and my life a testimony. Help those around me see Your goodness and believe that You sent Jesus. Amen.

11:43.devotion: After praying, Jesus cries out with a loud voice, commanding Lazarus to come forth from the tomb. This moment follows His conversation with the Father, showing that the miracle flows from God's power. The loud voice ensures everyone hears the command, and the command itself demonstrates Christ's authority even over death.
11:43.reflection: What tomb in your life have you assumed is sealed beyond the reach of Jesus' voice?
11:43.action: Name one dead or dormant hope—relationship, faith, courage—and ask Jesus in prayer to speak life into it today.
11:43.prayer: Lord Jesus, Your voice called Lazarus from the grave, and nothing is beyond Your reach. Speak into the places in my life that feel dead or hopeless. Awaken what has fallen silent, and let me hear You call. Amen.

11:44.devotion: Lazarus emerges from the tomb still bound in graveclothes, his face wrapped in cloth. Alive but restricted, he cannot free himself. Jesus turns to the bystanders and says, 'Loose him, and let him go.' The miracle invites human participation: the community is called to remove the remaining bindings so the restored man can live freely.
11:44.reflection: Whose bindings might God be inviting you to help loosen—through forgiveness, encouragement, or practical help?
11:44.action: Offer one freeing act today: forgive a debt, write an encouraging note, or practically help someone weighed down by a burden.
11:44.prayer: Lord, You bring life, and You invite us to join Your work. Show me someone still bound by grief, guilt, or hardship. Make me willing to do the humble work of loosening what holds them. Amen.

11:45.devotion: Many who had come to comfort Mary witnessed Jesus raising Lazarus and believed in Him. The sign accomplished its purpose: seeing Christ's power led to genuine faith. This verse reminds us that God works in visible ways, and witnesses must respond. Some saw and believed; the miracle demanded a verdict from every observer.
11:45.reflection: When God has worked in your life, have you responded with belief, or simply moved on unchanged?
11:45.action: Recall a specific answered prayer or providential moment this month, and write down how it deepened your trust in Jesus.
11:45.prayer: Father, open my eyes to see Your work around me. Don't let me witness Your goodness and remain unmoved. Strengthen my belief in Jesus, and let what I have seen shape how I live today. Amen.

11:46.devotion: Not everyone who saw the miracle responded with faith. Some went to the Pharisees and reported what Jesus did. The same event produced belief in some and opposition in others. This verse honestly portrays divided reactions to Jesus, showing that witnessing His works does not automatically soften hearts; responses to Christ vary, and hostility was already stirring.
11:46.reflection: What keeps a heart from believing even when the evidence of God's work is plain?
11:46.action: Ask God to reveal any hardness in your own heart, and confess one attitude or prejudice that resists what He is doing.
11:46.prayer: Lord, I confess that seeing is not always believing. Examine my heart and root out skepticism, pride, and fear that resist You. Give me a soft and honest heart that receives Your work with faith, not suspicion. Amen.

11:47.devotion: News of the miracle reaches the religious leaders, who convene a council. Rather than rejoicing or investigating honestly, they ask what to do about a man performing many signs. Their concern is not truth but control. This scene marks a turning point: Jesus' authentic miracles now trigger official deliberation about how to stop Him.
11:47.reflection: When God's work disrupts my plans or status, do I seek truth first, or do I move to protect what I'm comfortable losing?
11:47.action: Notice today where you resist change God may be bringing, and choose one small step of surrender instead of control.
11:47.prayer: Father, forgive me for the times I resist Your work because it threatens my comfort or position. Give me courage to welcome what You are doing, even when it unsettles my plans. Make me honest before You. Amen.

11:48.devotion: The council voices its fear: if they allow Jesus to continue, everyone will believe in Him, and the Romans will intervene and take away their place and nation. Political anxiety drives their reasoning. Ironically, they fear losing their position and people, and their attempt to preserve both by opposing Jesus will prove futile. Fear of loss clouded their judgment.
11:48.reflection: What fear of loss is currently shaping my decisions more than trust in God?
11:48.action: Identify one decision driven by fear of losing something, and prayerfully name the fear before God, asking Him to lead you instead.
11:48.prayer: Lord, You know how fear of losing security, reputation, or control grips me. Untangle my motives and free me from decisions ruled by anxiety. Teach me to trust You with what I cannot keep, and to follow Christ boldly. Amen.

11:49.devotion: Into the council's anxious debate, Caiaphas, the high priest that year, speaks up sharply, telling his colleagues they know nothing at all. His blunt interruption sets up the fateful counsel that follows in the next verses. The scene reveals the tension and urgency among the leaders, and God would sovereignly work even through this conflicted council.
11:49.reflection: Do I speak into tense situations with humility and care, or with sharpness that escalates conflict?
11:49.action: In your next tense conversation today, pause before speaking and choose one measured, gracious sentence instead of a sharp retort.
11:49.prayer: Father, guard my tongue in tense moments. Keep me from words that wound or inflame, and give me wisdom to speak with humility. Work Your purposes even through human conflict, and make me an instrument of Your peace. Amen.

11:50.devotion: After Jesus raised Lazarus, the religious leaders met in fear that Jesus' growing fame would provoke Rome. Caiaphas argued coldly that one man should die so the nation might be spared. His political calculation was selfish, yet God would weave even this counsel into His plan of salvation through Christ's death.
11:50.reflection: Have I ever seen God bring purpose out of words or plans that were meant for harm?
11:50.action: Today, write down one painful or unjust situation in your life and prayerfully ask God to redeem it for good.
11:50.prayer: Father, You are never defeated by human schemes. When people act out of fear or selfishness, Your purposes still stand. Help me trust Your greater plan, and keep me from cold, calculating hearts. I rest in the saving work of Jesus. Amen.

11:51.devotion: John explains that Caiaphas did not speak merely from his own reasoning. As high priest that year, he unknowingly prophesied truth: Jesus would die for the nation. God can speak through unlikely voices, and the office Caiaphas abused pointed, despite himself, to the true sacrifice to come.
11:51.reflection: Am I listening humbly enough for God to speak through unexpected people or circumstances?
11:51.action: Today, reread a conversation that surprised you this week and ask God in prayer what He might be saying through it.
11:51.prayer: Lord, You spoke through Caiaphas though he opposed You. Your wisdom outruns every human plan. Give me ears to hear Your truth wherever it comes, and guard my own mouth from proud, careless words. Thank You that Jesus died for us. Amen.

11:52.devotion: The high priest's unintended prophecy stretched further than Israel: Jesus would die not for one nation only, but to gather into one all God's scattered children. Christ's death would unite people from every place into one family. What Caiaphas meant as political arithmetic, God meant as a worldwide gathering of His own.
11:52.reflection: Who is different from me that Christ died for, and am I treating them as family?
11:52.action: Today, reach out warmly to one believer whose background, culture, or church differs from yours, and encourage them.
11:52.prayer: Father, thank You that Jesus died not for one people only, but to gather Your scattered children into one. Break down the walls I build between myself and others. Make me a peacemaker who welcomes all who belong to You. Amen.

11:53.devotion: From that day, the council resolved to put Jesus to death. A miracle that should have produced faith instead hardened unbelief into a murder plot. The passage honestly shows how resistance to God can calcify, and how darkness often escalates when confronted with the light it refuses to receive.
11:53.reflection: Where might I be resisting truth God has already placed clearly before me?
11:53.action: Today, identify one conviction you have been avoiding, confess it honestly to God, and take one small obedient step.
